paper_title: Do Probing and Steering Favor the Same Directions Within and Across Language Models?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A direction in a language model's hidden state can be used to probe whether a concept is present or to steer the model toward it. Although probe directions are often reused for steering, the direction that best detects a concept need not be the one that best changes it. We study this distinction in three instruction-tuned models from different families. We construct a one-parameter family of directions ranging from a covariance-adjusted discriminant to the mean difference, and evaluate probing and additive steering, which adds the direction to the hidden state, along the family at a fixed side effect. For truthfulness and sentiment, in every model, the best probe is not the best steering direction: steering consistently favors directions closer to the mean difference. This separation holds across 59 of 60 layer-model-concept combinations in a layer sweep, with matched probe and steering texts in all six model-concept combinations, and under a rotation-based steering operator. The exact steering optimum is less stable: for sentiment, an intermediate direction produces a 27-56% stronger steering effect than the mean difference, but this gain shrinks or disappears with matched texts and depends on the layer and the operator. The two roles also transfer differently across models. A probe transferred by a linear map fitted on neutral text retains 81-91% of the target model's above-chance probing performance, while the transferred mean difference retains less of its steering effect in 11 of 12 model pairs. This is a consistent tendency, although our predefined criteria classify only three pairs, and nine remain inconclusive. Finally, as an application on PopQA, steering toward "unknown" increases abstention by 18-44 percentage points on uncertain errors, versus 2-5 on confident errors, while rarely correcting errors in cases where a correct answer is reachable.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: A language models hidden state can be used, without changing the models weights, to probe for concept or to steer the model toward it. direction can predict concept well because it exploits variation correlated with the concept, without being the direction along which the model is most effectively changed. Steering methods nevertheless often reuse probe direction, for example, the reading vector of representation engineering [Zou et al., 2023]. Park et al. [2024] relate the representations used for probing and for steering through causal inner product, which raises an empirical question: does the direction that probes concept best also steer it best in the ordinary geometry of the hidden state? Earlier comparisons put trained probe against the mean difference, two fixed directions, and find that the mean difference can steer better [Li et al., 2023, Marks and Tegmark, 2024] and that the two can detect equally well but intervene differently [Wu et al., 2025]. Related code and interactive paper page in http://afshn.com/research/probing-vs-steering Preprint. In contrast to these two-endpoint comparisons, which show which of the two directions works better for each operation at chosen steering strength, we ask where between them each operation works best, at fixed side effect on unrelated text, so that no direction gains only by perturbing the model more. We therefore construct continuous family of directions that extends from covarianceadjusted discriminant to the mean difference, the direction commonly used for steering, and we measure probing and steering along the whole family at fixed side effect, in three model families, and carry each role across models under its own transfer law (Figure 1). Figure 1: Hidden states of one layer of LLM A. µ joins the two class means; the best probe wτ is tilted away from it by the within-class covariance, and the family wλ runs between them. Probing reads wh; steering adds ahw. The paper also asks how these two transfer across language models. The distinction matters most when representations are compared across models. Recent work reports convergence between independently trained models [Huh et al., 2024], but whether two models agree on concept may depend on whether the concept is read or changed. linear map between two models carries steering direction forward, whereas probe has to be carried by the transpose of the reverse map (Section 2.2). Each role can therefore be transferred under its own law, which turns representational alignment into functional question: do models agree more on how concept is read than on how it is changed? Our two main results concern the split between the roles. First, along continuous family of directions and at fixed side effect, the direction that probes concept best is not the one that steers it best. This holds in all six combinations of model and concept at the main layer, also with matched probe and steering texts, and, in separate analyses, at 59 of 60 combinations of layer, model and concept for truthfulness and sentiment in layer sweep and in the four cases where rotation-based operator reaches the same side effect (Appendices M, and G). Second, between models of three families, each role carried under its own law, probes keep most of their performance while the mean difference keeps less of its steering effect in most pairs. secondary result is that where steering works best, and whether an intermediate direction beats the mean difference, depends on the concept, the layer, the operator, and the texts. As an application, using an error taxonomy adapted from Orgad et al. [2025], we show that steering toward unknown turns uncertain errors into abstentions far more readily than confident ones, while the probe and steering directions for this concept are less clearly separated than for truthfulness and sentiment, and gating by the probe protects correct answers but passes our test only in Qwen.

sections.content: Two research questions outline this study. We ask whether probing and steering favor the same directions, within model and across models (RQ1), and whether this distinction helps to separate wrong answers by whether correct answer is reachable and to steer the model toward abstention (RQ2). Section 2.1 defines the family of directions and how probing, steering, and their side effect are measured on it; Section 2.2 describes how directions are carried between models; Sections 2.3 and 2.4 present the hypotheses that the experiments evaluate. 2.1 Background and Definitions Probe score. We treat each concept as binary and use texts labeled for its presence (y = 1) or absence (y = 0), for example, true TruthfulQA answers and positive Yelp reviews labeled = 1. Let Rd, with the hidden size, be the hidden state at the last token of the text after fixed layer ℓ (Section 3.1). This is the residual-stream vector at that token, the sum of the tokens input embedding and the outputs of all attention and feed-forward blocks up to and including layer ℓ. We define probe as direction in the space of h, and its probe score as wh. Appendix shows that reading at the last token separates the labels better than max pooling over the tokens, the reading used by Wu et al. [2025, Sec. 3.2], for both concepts and all three models. Below we define 2 the family of directions and compute each direction once, in closed form, from the (h, y) pairs of an estimation subset. Mean difference. Let µ1 = E[h = 1] and µ0 = E[h = 0] be the mean representations of the two classes. For each PopQA question (Section 3.1), with dont know allowed, the model gives one greedy answer and five sampled answers, each judged correct, wrong, or an abstention. C0 is the set of questions whose greedy answer is correct. C1 is the set of questions whose greedy answer is wrong although at least one sample is correct, that is, errors for which correct answer is reachable under our decoding; we call them knowledge-available errors for short. C2, the uncertain errors, and C3, the confident errors, are the sets of questions with no correct answer among the six whose wrong greedy answer is repeated in at most two or in at least four of the five samples; Cm holds the remaining such errors, repeated in exactly three samples, and AK and AU the greedy abstentions with and without correct answer among the six (Table 5 in Appendix I). Every direction is compared with 5 random direction at the same K. Across models, we also measure, without hypothesis, whether the models agree on which questions have reachable answer and whether their probes and directions for unknown transfer.

sections.title: 3 Experiments
sections.content: 3.1 Models and Datasets We study LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3.5-9B (the post-trained checkpoint), and Gemma-3-12B-it, with raw prompts and no chat template. We abbreviate these as LLaMA, Qwen, and Gemma, and in tables as L, Q, and G; figure labels omit the -Instruct and -it suffixes. For each model, we use layer at about 0.44 of its depth, layer 14 of 32, 14 of 32, and 21 of 48, respectively (layers counted from 0). We chose this depth in advance. sweep over ten depths in all three models and for all three concepts (Appendix M) supports it: averaged over the concepts, the probing AUROC at this layer is within 0.004 of the best layer in every model, and H1a holds at 59 of the 60 combinations of layer, model, and concept for truthfulness and sentiment, the two concepts with steering sweep. For truthfulness, we use TruthfulQA [Lin et al., 2022], each question followed by the answers of its multi-true list (MC2), labeled true or false (Appendix K); for sentiment, we use 2,000 Yelp reviews (1,000 positive and 1,000 negative) [Zhang et al., 2015]. Both datasets are split 50/25/25 into an estimation subset and two held-out sets, on which the directions are evaluated. For RQ2, we use 4,000 PopQA questions [Mallen et al., 2023]; the concept unknown is used only in this experiment, with labels taken from each models own answers (Section 3.4). Neutral WikiText-2 sentences [Merity et al., 2017] measure the side effect and serve to fit the maps between models. 3.2 Probing and Steering Evaluation (cid:80) For each model and concept, we estimate µ0, µ1 and ΣW on the estimation subset, with the pooled estimate ΣW = 1 i: yi=c(hi ˆµc)(hi ˆµc), which weights the two class covariances n2 by their sample shares as in Section 2.1, and compute wλ for 13 values of λ/τ , spaced by half decade from 103 to 103, adding µ as the end point. sections.title: 5 Related Work
sections.content: Probing and steering concepts. unified analysis of steering methods favors the mean of differences [Im and Li, 2025], and ridge-regularized probes have been used to obtain concept directions for steering [Gao et al., 2026]. Closest to our setting, Cheng and Amo Alonso [2026] and Hedström et al. [2025] steer along probes own direction with strength set per token in closed form, in several model families; the first notes that linear decodability does not guarantee linear controllability, which agrees with our finding that the best probe is not the best steering direction. These works vary the strength along one direction; none of them, nor the comparisons cited in Section 1, varies the 9 direction itself along the family between the probe and the mean difference and measures probing and steering at each point of it at fixed side effect. Concept erasure removes several directions [Ravfogel et al., 2020] or, in closed form, the subspace that linear classifiers use [Belrose et al., 2023]; we study single directions. Representation transfer. Learned maps carry objects from one model to another: affine stitches transfer sparse autoencoders, sparse probes and steering vectors between sizes of one family [Chen et al., 2025], affine maps and autoencoders transfer steering vectors between sizes and across families [Bello et al., 2025, Oozeer et al., 2025], and an affine map on final hidden states lets one models states be decoded through anothers output head [Gorbett and Jana, 2026]. These works move one kind of object at time, mostly steering vectors, and judge it by the behavior it produces in the target; where probes and steering vectors are both moved [Chen et al., 2025], the two are tested on different pairs of models, so their transfer cannot be compared. We instead move the same family of directions in both roles between the same three model families, in all six ordered pairs, each role under its own law and both measured against the targets own direction at fixed side effect, with the wrong law and an orthogonal map as controls; this shows that probes transfer more reliably than steering directions and that each role transfers well only under its own law. Knowledge awareness. Whether model knows an answer can be predicted from its own judgment [Kadavath et al., 2022] or its internal states [Gottesman and Geva, 2024], and errors made despite knowledge can be distinguished from errors caused by missing knowledge [Simhi et al., 2024, Orgad et al., 2025]. probe on the hidden state before generation can also stand in for sampling-based semantic uncertainty [Han et al., 2024]. Other studies examine confident errors and associationdriven hallucinations [Simhi et al., 2025, Cheang et al., 2026], steer knowledge awareness or gate the intervention [Ferrando et al., 2025, Kumaran et al., 2026, Hedström et al., 2025, Lee et al., 2025], or train steering toward abstention into the weights of one layer [Yang et al., 2026]. We instead study what steering toward unknown does to each type of error, and how its probe and steering direction differ and transfer. As an application, this steering reduces hallucinations by turning wrong answers into abstentions, mostly the uncertain ones, at small cost in correct answers.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: In each model we test, the direction of the family that probes concept best does not steer it best: probing peaks near λ = τ and steering further toward the mean difference, in all six main combinations, also with matched texts, at 59 of 60 combinations for truthfulness and sentiment in layer sweep, and in the four cases where rotation reaches the same side effect. The two roles also separate across models. Each carried under its own law, probes keep most of their performance, for unknown as well, while the mean difference keeps less of its steering effect in most pairs; under maps fitted on neutral text, the tested models agree more on how concept is read than on how it is changed, although part of the steering loss may come from the maps. Where steering works best is less stable: whether an intermediate direction beats the mean difference depends on the concept, the layer, the operator, and the texts (Appendices F, and M). On PopQA, steering toward unknown turns uncertain errors into abstentions far more readily than confident ones; the probe for unknown steers almost as strongly as the mean difference in Qwen and Gemma, and gating by the probe protects correct answers but passes our test only in Qwen. These results come from three concepts and three models, with the main analyses at one layer per model; the twelve ordered pairs of the cross-model experiments share models and are therefore not independent, and all results concern single directions under additive and rotational steering. Appendix lists the further limitations. Probe directions should therefore not be reused for steering without checking how well they steer.

sections.title: A Limitations
sections.content: Scope of the evidence. All results come from three concepts (truthfulness, sentiment, and unknown on PopQA) and three instruction-tuned models (LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma-312B), and the main analyses use one layer per model. The layer sweep of Appendix covers the probing and steering of RQ1 only; the steering of RQ2, including the H2b(iii) and H2c verdicts, was run at the papers layer alone, so we do not know how those verdicts change with depth. Other concepts, base models, or larger models may behave differently. The cross-model pairs are not independent. Three models give six ordered pairs, and two concepts give twelve. Every pair shares its source or its target with four other pairs, so property of one model appears in four of the twelve points at once; for example, the poor probing of Gemmas own mean difference affects every pair into or out of Gemma. Counts such as 11 of 12 pairs therefore describe pattern in three models and should not be read as twelve separate confirmations. The cross-model comparison also uses only the unmatched probe and steering texts of Section 3.2; the matched-text control of Appendix was run within models only. Single directions and two operators. We study one direction at time, drawn from single one-parameter family, and two ways of applying it: addition and gated rotation. We do not study subspaces, nonlinear probes, sparse-autoencoder features, or steering operators learned from data, and the conclusions may not carry over to them. The rotation operator is gated by the states cosine with the direction, and its side-effect budget is set on neutral text where the gate opens less often than on task text; its H1b verdicts therefore mix the effect of the rotation with that of the gate (Appendix G). What is measured. Steering is measured by the change of an answer margin (truthfulness, unknown) or of word log-odds (sentiment), not by task accuracy, so direction that moves the margin need not change which answer the model gives. Probing is measured by AUROC. The two transfer ratios ρprobe and ρsteer therefore compare different quantities, an AUROC above chance and steering effect, and their comparison is approximate. The side effect is the next-token KL divergence on 200 neutral WikiText-2 sentences, not on the task prompts or over generated continuations, and the budget κ0 is anchored to the mean difference at one strength; the post hoc check over sixteen-fold range of budgets (Appendix D) reads saved curves and has no intervals. Maps and estimates. The maps between models are fitted on neutral text and fit the concept texts less well (R2 of 0.130.47 against 0.480.70 on held-out neutral text), so part of the loss of carried steering direction may come from the map rather than from the models, and no pair can be called neither shared. ΣW is estimated once per model and concept from fewer examples than dimensions, so the estimate is singular and the small-λ end of the family is the part of µ outside the span of the training states rather than the Fisher discriminant (Appendix B). RQ2 labels. The cases of RQ2 are defined from the greedy answer and five sampled answers, so they capture whether correct answer is reachable under this sampling, not whether the model knows the fact; question whose correct answer appears with probability in one sample is missed by all five with probability (1 p)5, which biases the no correct answer class toward questions the model could sometimes answer. Knowledge-available errors (C1) are rare, 71, 33, and 35 questions, so the H2b(ii) verdicts rest on point estimates with wide intervals. Prompts are plain text without the models chat templates, and Qwens thinking tokens are handled by token budget (Appendix I). Truthfulness data. Truthfulness is tested on TruthfulQA alone, and its directions are computed and evaluated on the same dataset, so gain of an intermediate direction cannot be separated from gain of fitting the test distribution. Truthfulness probes trained on one dataset can generalize poorly to others [Liu et al., 2024], and we did not test whether the directions of this paper transfer to other truthfulness data.

TruthfulQA. TruthfulQA consists of 817 questions; the multiple-choice lists of its release contain 5,882 reference answers (2,585 true, 3,297 false). The dataset release provides two multiple-choice lists per question. The multi-true list (MC2) contains all reference answers of the question, of which one or more are true; it corresponds to the multiple-choice task of Lin et al. For MC1, model selects the answer to which it assigns the highest likelihood, and the score is the share of questions for which this answer is the true one. After normalization (lowercase, punctuation and articles removed), an answer abstains if it is empty or contains phrase from fixed list (for example dont know, not sure, no idea); otherwise it is correct if it contains one of PopQAs possible answers (answers of at most three characters must match whole word), and wrong otherwise. Qwen3.5 sometimes opens reasoning block (<think>) instead of answering. For such continuations, we generate up to 384 new tokens and take the answer from the text after the closing </think>; if the block does not close within this budget, or the answer is only chat role word, the answer is invalid, which counts as neither correct, wrong, nor an abstention. This leaves 121 of Qwens 4,000 greedy answers (3%) and 187 of its 20,000 samples invalid; LLaMA and Gemma produce no invalid answers. Questions whose greedy answer is invalid form their own case (INV) and are not part of C0C3. For the entropy baseline, Qwens first answer token is taken after closed reasoning block (107 questions); for 123 questions whose block does not close, the entropy stays at the first generated token. The steered runs use the same budget, so steered continuation that opens reasoning block is also extended; invalid continuations count as neither an abstention nor correct answer, and at the anchor strength µ leaves 108 of them (17 among the 123 C2 questions) against 124 in the unsteered rerun. Reading Hent after closed block puts it at different position than the probe for 107 questions; excluding them, its AUROC on C2 against C3 rises from 0.69 to 0.84 and on the H2a(i) contrasts from 0.59 to 0.62 and from 0.73 to 0.74, so this does not favor the probe in any contrast. Reading position: last token versus pooling probe is obtained in two steps. First, estimation: from the hidden states of the training texts, µ and ΣW are computed and from them the direction (Sections 2.1 and 3.2); this is done once, and the result is fixed vector. Second, scoring: for held-out text, some of its hidden states are multiplied by and the products are combined into one number, the probe score, from which the AUROC is computed. In all our main experiments both steps use the hidden state at the last token of the text. AxBench [Wu et al., 2025, Sec. 3.2] instead scores every token of text and keeps the maximum. We compare three ways of turning text into one probe score. The first is the one used in all our main experiments: the direction is estimated from the hidden states at the last token of the texts, and held-out text is scored by whT at its last token. The second is max pooling, the scoring used by AxBench [Wu et al., 2025, Sec. 3.2]: every token of the text is scored, wht for = 1, . . . , , and the largest score is kept; In the second variant, the vector is computed once from last-token states, as in the first variant (ours), so the direction is the same in both variants. It is then, however, multiplied with the hidden state of every token and the largest product is kept, so the same text can receive different score in the two variants. The hidden states at the intermediate tokens have their own class means and within-class spread, and direction estimated from them would differ from the one estimated at the last token; no variant estimates µ and ΣW from all token positions. The third is mean pooling: the hidden states of the text are averaged into h, µ and ΣW are reestimated from these averaged states, and held-out text is scored by wh; here both the estimation and the scoring change. In the second variant the direction estimated at the last token is applied to every token, whose class means and within-class covariance can differ from those at the last token; no variant estimates µ and ΣW from all token positions. Only the tokens that carry the concept are pooled: the answer for TruthfulQA and the whole review for sentiment; special tokens are excluded. Each variant chooses its best direction of the family on the first held-out split, and the choices are compared on the second split with paired bootstrap that resamples questions or reviews (1,000 resamples). Significance is corrected with Holms method 24 over all 18 comparisons we ran, including third variant, directions computed from mean states but scored by max pooling, which is omitted here and was never better than the last token. Table 10 gives the held-out AUROC of the last-token reading on the second held-out split and, for each pooling, the difference to it (negative: the last token is better), with paired bootstrap 95% intervals. After correction, the last token was significantly better than the alternative in 8 of the 12 comparisons and never significantly worse. Max pooling, the scoring used by AxBench, was worse in all six cases and lost up to 0.10 AUROC on truthfulness. Mean pooling gave slightly higher AUROC for sentiment in all three models (+0.006 to +0.015), but none of these differences are significant after correction. Sentiment is spread over the whole review rather than concentrated at its end, which may be why averaging does not hurt there, while it lowers the AUROC for truthfulness. The loss under max pooling therefore shows that direction fitted at the last token does not transfer to scoring every token, not that token-level estimation would do worse; directions estimated across all pooled positions were not run. sections.content: The paper reads and steers every model at about 0.44 of its depth (Section 3.1). This appendix gives the basis for that choice: how well each concept can be probed, and how strongly µ steers it, at other depths. To check this, we repeat the RQ1 measurements at ten relative depths, from 1/8 to 7/8 of the layers: layers 4, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 24 and 28 of 32 in LLaMA and Qwen, and 6, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30, 36 and 42 of 48 in Gemma. The data, splits, and steering prompts are those of Section 3.2, and the probe and the steering intervention always use the same layer. To keep the computing time of the sweep manageable, with ten depths for each model and concept and six steering strengths per direction, the family has six members instead of fourteen, λ {103, 0.1, 1, 10, 100} τ and µ. Values at the papers layer can therefore differ slightly from those of Section 4.1 when the main runs best direction lies at grid point the sweep lacks: the best AUROC does so only for sentiment in LLaMA (0.980 against 0.981) and Qwen (0.964 against 0.966), whose best probe sits at 3τ , and the H1b ratios, whose λ is chosen on the coarser grid, by up to 0.08 (truthfulness in Gemma, 0.99 against 1.07). Each layer has its own budget κ0, the of µ at = 0.1 (0.01 for Gemma) at that layer. For RQ2, we sweep probing only. The PopQA labels do not depend on the layer, so we read the prompts of all 4,000 questions at the ten layers and compute the cross-fitted probe of Section 3.4 at each of them, with 95% bootstrap intervals (200 resamples). Steering toward unknown was not swept. sections.content: This appendix provides additional figures supporting the results in Section 4. Each figure is followed by short description of what it shows. N.1 Probing and steering within models Figure 6: Probing (top, held-out AUROC) and steering at κ0 in each concepts own units (bottom) against λ/τ . The shapes match Figure 2, but the size of the effects differs between models. 28 Gemma shows the split most clearly: its mean difference hardly separates the classes (AUROC 0.596 for truthfulness and 0.631 for sentiment), yet steering along it still changes the models behavior: direction can be nearly useless as probe and still steer. Figure 2 divides every steering effect by that of µ, which makes the models comparable but hides how large the effects are. Figure 6 shows the raw values against λ/τ , with the steering effect in nats of answer margin for truthfulness and as the change of the log-odds of positive versus negative words for sentiment. The shape is the same in all three models: probing peaks near λ = τ , while steering rises from almost nothing at the probe end to its maximum further to the right. For truthfulness, the probe end barely steers at all; the effect stays close to zero up to about λ = 0.1τ . The models differ in how much they move: for truthfulness, Qwen and Gemma move the answer margin about twice as much as LLaMA at the same side effect, and for sentiment, LLaMA moves the most. The steep drop of Gemmas AUROC toward µ is the near-chance probing of its mean difference discussed above. Figure 7: Each direction of the family at its probing AUROC (horizontal) and its steering effect relative to µ (vertical). No curve ends in the upper right corner, so no direction is best at both. In Figure 7, lines connect the directions in the order of the family, bubbles grow from the probe end to µ, the ring marks µ, the small dot marks λ = τ , and the dashed line marks the steering effect of µ. If one direction were best at both tasks, the curve of each model would end in the upper right corner. It does not. For truthfulness, each curve runs up along the right edge and then bends to the left: the directions that probe best (AUROC about 0.96) steer weakly, and the directions that steer best probe somewhat worse. For sentiment, the strongest steering (up to 1.6 times that of µ, for Qwen) comes from directions that probe well but not best, and µ itself lies to the left of them. Gemmas ring sits near an AUROC of 0.6 in both panels: its mean difference steers, but hardly probes. N.2 Probing and steering across models Figure 3 shows the H1c comparison of Section 4.1. As controls, we also steer with µA carried by the probe law, BAµA, probe with the transferred direction under the steering law and under an orthogonal Procrustes map (used for probing only; all other transfer results use the ridge maps), steer with the sources probe end carried by the steering law, and compare cos(MABµA, µB) with null in which As labels are permuted; Table 16 gives these per pair. Each point is one ordered pair sourcetarget (L = LLaMA, = Qwen, = Gemma) for one concept, and the dashed diagonal marks equal ratios. The shaded corners are probe-shared (ρprobe 0.8, ρsteer < 0.5), steering-shared (the reverse), both-shared (both 0.8) and neither-shared (both < 0.5). All pairs lie at the right edge, but most lie below the diagonal. Three caveats temper this reading. First, ρprobe and ρsteer are ratios of different quantities, an AUROC above chance and steering effect, so comparing them is only approximate. In particular, AUROC saturates: under the Gaussian model of Appendix B, AUROC = Φ(d/ 2) with the standardized separation, and at target AUROC of 0.960.98 probe that loses third of its still keeps about 85% of the AUROC above chance. Recomputed on the scale from the same held-out AUROCs, ρprobe falls to 0.650.79 and exceeds ρsteer in 9 of 12 pairs instead of 11: all six truthfulness pairs hold, while for sentiment LLaMAQwen (0.76 against 0.93), LLaMAGemma (0.66 against 0.72) and GemmaQwen (0.79 against 0.81) no longer do. For unknown, whose target probes lie further from the ceiling (AUROC 0.920.94), the ratio is 0.820.92 against steering ratio of 0.300.79, so all six pairs hold on either scale. Second, the maps are fitted on neutral text and fit the concept texts less well (R2 of 0.130.47, against 0.480.70 on held-out neutral text; Table 16). Part of the loss in steering may therefore come from the map rather than from the models, and for the same reason no pair can be called neither shared. Third, ρprobe and ρsteer measure what carried direction does in the target, how well it reads the concept and how strongly it pushes the model, not how close it lies to the targets own direction; carried direction can do the job while pointing away from the targets own µ. The measure is therefore functional rather than geometric. In 10 of 12 pairs, the mapped µ is closer to the targets own µ than mean difference computed with permuted labels (cosine 0.530.81, against 95th null percentile of 0.120.66). In the two sentiment pairs into Gemma, however, it is no closer to Gemmas own µ than the permuted-label null (cosine 0.17 and 0.02) and still steers at 0.72 and 0.70 of its effect. The disagreement is confined to the mean-difference end. Along the family, the carried source direction MAGwA,λ and Gemmas own wG,λ have positive cosine that rises from 0.20 at the probe end to 0.50 at 32τ (from LLaMA) and 0.64 at 100τ (from Qwen), and turns negative only at µ. Along the family, the carried source direction MAGwA,λ and Gemmas own wG,λ have positive cosine that rises from 0.20 at the probe end to 0.50 at 32τ (from LLaMA) and 0.64 at 100τ (from Qwen), and turns negative only at µ. Gemmas own sentiment µ probes at an AUROC of 0.63 (Appendix N), so most of its length lies along directions that do not carry the concept; the carried µA points away from those directions and with the regularized ones that carry it, which is probably why it steers the right way.
